deep.reconstruction:
Context: §28 of the 'Fragmenta ex Adversariis deprompta' (Opera Posthuma, 1862; marginal source 'A. m. T. II p.170-171'). For a prime p=2n+1, Euler looks for x such that the residues of 1, x, x^2, ..., x^{2n} mod p run through all of 1..2n. In modern terms these are primitive roots. This page continues the worked examples and then gives general 'Reflexiones'.

(III, cont.) p=7. Euler had x=3, giving the cycle 1,3,2,6,4,5,1. Any power x^λ with gcd(λ,6)=1 also works. For λ=5, 3^5 ≡ 5 (mod 7), giving 1,5,4,6,2,3,1. This is the previous cycle reversed, because 5 ≡ 3^{-1}. General remark: the reversed series always works, since x^{-1} is a primitive root whenever x is.

(IV) p=11, n=5, x=2: powers 2^k mod 11 for k=0..10 are 1,2,4,8,5,10,9,7,3,6,1. The second printed row 1..9 indexes the exponents of the interior terms. The reversed cycle comes from x=6 = 2^{-1} = 2^9: 1,6,3,7,9,10,5,8,4,2,1. The other primitive roots are x^3, x^7, x^9, i.e. 8, 7, 6 (exponents coprime to 10). For x=8: 1,8,9,6,4,10,3,2,5,7,1. Its reverse comes from x=7 = 8^{-1}.

(V) p=13, n=6, x=2: 1,2,4,8,3,6,12,11,9,5,10,7,1. The other primitive roots are 2^5, 2^7, 2^11 = 6, 11, 7. For x=6: 1,6,10,8,9,2,12,7,3,5,4,11,1.

General reflections.
(1) x^n ≡ -1 = p-1 = 2n. Reason: (x^n)^2 = x^{2n} ≡ 1, so x^n ≡ ±1. My addition: x^n ≢ 1 because x has full order 2n.
(2) If x^λ ≡ a, then x^{n+λ} ≡ -a ≡ p-a = 2n+1-a. So the second half of the cycle consists of the complements of the first half, and it suffices to compute up to the middle.
(3) Define α ≡ 1/a (mod p), i.e. α = (mp+1)/a for the integer m making it whole. For p=13: a = 2,3,4,5,6,7 gives α = 7,9,10,8,11,2. Remark: the inverse of a complement is the complement of the inverse, (-a)^{-1} = -(a^{-1}).
(4) If x^λ ≡ a, then:
- x^{2n-λ} ≡ α, since x^λ · x^{2n-λ} = x^{2n} ≡ 1;
- x^{n+λ} ≡ p-a;
- x^{n-λ} ≡ p-α.
Thus one term determines four.

Illustration p=19, n=9. Euler tabulates x^0..x^17 in terms of a=x, b=x^2, c=x^3, d=x^4 and their inverses α,β,γ,δ:
- x^9 = 18;
- x^{9+k} = 19 - (x^k);
- x^{18-k} = inverse of x^k;
- x^{9-k} = p - inverse of x^k.
With a=2: b=4, c=8, d=16, α=10, β=5, γ=12, δ=6. This yields (on the next page) the full cycle 1,2,4,8,16,13,7,14,9,18,17,15,11,3,6,12,5,10.
errors: No arithmetic errors found; all listed cycles, primitive roots and inverses check out.

Reflexion 1 is slightly incomplete as written ('x^n = √1, ergo x^n = -1'). It needs x^n ≠ 1 (full order of x), and the fact that ±1 are the only square roots of 1 modulo a prime. Both are implicit in the setup.
The existence of such an x for every prime p is asserted on the basis of examples only ('uti ex sequentibus exemplis patebit'); no proof is given.

results.what: For every prime p some x has powers running through all nonzero residues; the other generators are x^λ with gcd(λ,p-1)=1, so there are φ(p-1) of them.
results.modern_name: Existence and count of primitive roots modulo a prime
results.usually_credited_to: Euler (term 'radix primitiva', E449, 1773/74; incomplete proof); Lambert 1769 (statement); Legendre 1785; Gauss, Disquisitiones 1801 (first complete proof)

results.what: x^{(p-1)/2} ≡ -1 for a primitive root x, hence x^{n+λ} ≡ -x^λ: second half of the cycle is the complement of the first half
results.modern_name: Index arithmetic / Euler's criterion for a primitive root (primitive root is a non-residue)

results.what: Inverse of a primitive root is a primitive root (retrograde series); ind(a^{-1}) = (p-1) - ind(a); ind(-a^{-1}) = n - ind(a); one term determines four

deep.surprise_reason: This is Euler's well-known work on primitive roots, contemporary with E449. The fragment is from his notebooks, published in the 1862 Opera Posthuma. It is worked examples and elementary index properties already associated with Euler.

transcription_corrections: Transcription is essentially faithful to the image.
The index rows under the p=11 and p=13 progressions (1..9 and 1..11) mark exponents of interior terms. They are not part of the series.
In Reflexion 1 the printed text reads 'x^n = √1, ergo x^n = -1 = p-1 = 2n', as transcribed.
